summary: Cream-brick 1866 tower on Simmons Island, Kenosha's harbor light until 1906. Now a museum with a replica lantern; keepers include the Merrill women and Louis De Diemar.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination says the Lighthouse Board discontinued the tower light in 1903 and moved its flash to the breakwater; LighthouseFriends gives 23 May 1906 as the permanent end, and the Lighthouse Digest gives 28 May 1906. The story gives both dates.

LighthouseFriends dates the restoration of the keeper's dwelling from 2004; the Kenosha History Center says the county historical society and the city began restoring it in 2001 (plan 2002, grants 2004). The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left open: (1) focal height: 76 ft (23 m) in the nomination and the Society's record vs 74 ft (focal plane above the lake, from the History Center); the facts field uses 23.2 m. (2) Lantern removal: 1913 (LighthouseFriends, History Center) vs cupola and lantern removed 1959 (nomination). (3) Storm mast: 15-ft steel tower (nomination) vs 25-ft tripod (LighthouseFriends, History Center). (4) Coast Guard: 1940 (LighthouseFriends), 1942 (nomination), city owns 1955 (LighthouseFriends); the nomination also says the weather tower stopped signals in 1953. (5) Dwelling addition: 1907 (nomination, Congress $2,500) vs 1908 (LighthouseFriends redbrick duplex addition). (6) The 1858 second tower appears only in LighthouseFriends; the History Center's 'third government lighthouse' supports it; the nomination mentions only the 1848 tower. (7) De Diemar's birthplace: Montreal (LighthouseFriends, Digest) vs Toronto in a county biography (RootsWeb transcription, not fetched: 403 on fetch). The Digest puts the battle at 'Perrysville, Missouri'; Perryville is in Kentucky and the story does not repeat that. (8) Digest's fog-signal anecdote about inspector J.M. Orchard is NOT used: the Digest does not say it happened at Kenosha, and this station had no fog signal (USLHS record: fog_signal_building false). (9) Merrill dismissal (1872): LighthouseFriends says newspapers tried to get the Merrills reinstated; Chronicling America searches for Merrill and Southport in Wisconsin 1871-73 returned no hits, so that detail rests on LighthouseFriends alone. (10) Lighthouse Board 1893 and 1901 volumes: the OCR is poor; the 1893 quote is from scan p. 21 (cleaner than p. 173); scan page numbers should be checked against the printed pages. (11) The 1866 Kenosha News inspection and 1941/1966 condition reports come only through the nomination; we did not read the newspapers. (12) The Life-Saving Service station at Kenosha (No. 13) is a separate station; its rescues are not attributed to the light. (13) Climbing: Wikipedia says the tower is open to climbers on some summer weekends; the 1989 nomination says the door is boarded. Not confirmed; the story says treat as closed. (14) The Kenosha North Pier light is another station on the map (us-wi-kenosha-north-pier); the other_stations link goes there. (15) Newspapers: two Chronicling America searches (Merrill, Southport, 1871-73) returned nothing. (16) Roster: all 44 lines are from the USLHS place page as printed by roster.py; no line is from another source. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the earlier story said no source read gave tower access; LighthouseFriends' visitor information says the dwelling and tower are open in season, and the story now says so and asks the museum about climbing. The 1858 tower count: the History Center's 'third government lighthouse' fits a second tower between 1848 and 1866, so the story no longer says the sources disagree on the count. The LighthouseFriends phrase on the 1996 beacon is paraphrased (copyrighted source). Names matched by position: none; the 1850 Miller date is from LighthouseFriends text, not an OCR table.
